text.p: McDonnell Douglas Corp said Monday it will not proceed with its plans to develop the MD-XX commercial jetliner due to a difficult pricing climate.
"We have decided that we are not going to proceed with the development of the proposed MD-XX airplane," said Tom Downey, spokesman for McDonnell Douglas.

"The combined investment isn't merited right now when you weigh it against the risk that is involved in making it a financial and market sucess," he said. "There is a lot of intensity in the climate of pricing out there right now."

McDonnell Douglas has been working on the plans for about six-months. The project worked on two versions of the MD-XX. One model of the plane had a seating capacity of about 300 but had a 20 percent greater range that the MD-11 allowing it to fly about 8,500 nautical miles.
The second "stretch" version was 31 feet longer than the MD-11 and could seat 375 passengers.

The plane required a new wing which analysts thought would have needed about $2 billion to develop with another $1 billion needed for infrastructure upgrades at Douglas Aircraft to build the jetliner.
Analysts said the aerospace giant had netted about 50 orders for the MD-XX.
Downey said McDonnell Douglas will focus on its niche market of 100-150 seat airplanes as well as cargo freighters.
"We're evaluating alternate strategies to ensure our long-term success in the market," Downey said.

Analysts said McDonnell balked at the investment needed to develop the range of aircraft it would need to compete with Boeing Co and Airbus Industrie in the commercial airplane market. McDonnell would have had to spend up to $15 billion over 10-15 years, analysts said.
"They will be looking for partners that would like to make major investments into (Douglas Aircraft)," said Paul Nisbet of JSA Research Inc.
"If they get that they could change their picture but they're not going to go it alone because of the tremendous investment involved," Nisbet said.
Analysts speculated that McDonnell Douglas may choose to sell Douglas Aircraft saying that Chief Executive Officer Harry Stonecipher would be ammenable to the idea if the price were right.

"I do recall Stonecipher ... saying if you can find a buyer willing to spend a premium price for commercial operations give me a ring, immediately," Nisbet said adding that "It probably isn't very saleable."
